claim: T cell expansion and differentiation are critically dependent on the transcription factor c-Myc (Myc).
source: T cell expansion and differentiation are critically dependent on the transcription factor c-Myc (Myc).
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by the study's findings and prior literature.

claim: Quantitative mass-spectrometry analysis of copy numbers per cell of >7000 proteins provides new understanding of the selective role of Myc in controlling the protein machinery that govern T cell fate.
source: Analysis of copy numbers per cell of >7000 proteins provides new understanding of the selective role of Myc in controlling the protein machinery that govern T cell fate.
evidence: The study performed quantitative mass-spectrometry identifying >7000 proteins as stated in the abstract and results.

claim: The data identify both Myc dependent and independent metabolic processes in immune activated T cells.
source: The data identify both Myc dependent and independent metabolic processes in immune activated T cells.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by proteomics data showing differential regulation.

claim: A primary function of Myc is to control expression of multiple amino acid transporters.
source: We uncover that a primary function of Myc is to control expression of multiple amino acid transporters and that loss of a single Myc-controlled amino acid transporter effectively phenocopies the impact of Myc deletion.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through proteomics and functional assays.

claim: Loss of a single Myc-controlled amino acid transporter effectively phenocopies the impact of Myc deletion.
source: We uncover that a primary function of Myc is to control expression of multiple amino acid transporters and that loss of a single Myc-controlled amino acid transporter effectively phenocopies the impact of Myc deletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative proteomics data between MyccKO and Slc7a5cKO T cells.

claim: Myc induction of amino acid transport is pivotal for subsequent bioenergetic and biosynthetic programs and licences T cell receptor driven proteome reprogramming.
source: This study provides a comprehensive map of how Myc selectively shapes T cell phenotypes, revealing that Myc induction of amino acid transport is pivotal for subsequent bioenergetic and biosynthetic programs and licences T cell receptor driven proteome reprogramming.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the comprehensive proteomics analysis.

claim: Immune activation transcriptionally reprograms T lymphocytes and initiates changes in cell metabolism and protein synthesis that are required for proliferation and effector differentiation.
source: Immune activation transcriptionally reprograms T lymphocytes and initiates changes in cell metabolism and protein synthesis that are required for proliferation and effector differentiation.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in immunology stated in the introduction.

claim: The transcription factor Myc has a necessary role in controlling T cell metabolism.
source: The signalling pathways that control T cell metabolism are not fully characterised but it has been shown that the transcription factor Myc has a necessary role (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2011).

claim: Myc is rapidly induced in response to engagement of the T cell antigen receptor (TCR).
source: In T cells, Myc is rapidly induced in response to engagement of the T cell antigen receptor (TCR) and Myc expression is then sustained by costimulatory receptors and cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2) (Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Heinzel et al., 2017; Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Myc expression is sustained by costimulatory receptors and cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2).
source: In T cells, Myc is rapidly induced in response to engagement of the T cell antigen receptor (TCR) and Myc expression is then sustained by costimulatory receptors and cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2) (Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Heinzel et al., 2017; Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The TCR acts as a digital switch for Myc mRNA expression, in that the strength of the antigen stimulus determines the frequency of T cells that switch on Myc mRNA expression.
source: The TCR acts as a digital switch for Myc mRNA expression, in that the strength of the antigen stimulus determines the frequency of T cells that switch on Myc mRNA expression (Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Preston et al., 2015.

claim: Constant phosphorylation on Thr58 by glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) and subsequent proteasomal degradation results in a short cellular half-life of Myc protein.
source: Antigen receptor, costimulation and cytokine driven processes also post-transcriptionally control Myc protein: constant phosphorylation on Thr58 by glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) and subsequent proteasomal degradation results in a short cellular half-life of Myc protein (Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Preston et al., 2015.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of Myc at Thr58, fuelled by the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway, blocks degradation and allows Myc to accumulate.
source: O-GlcNAcylation of Myc at this same residue (Chou et al., 1995), fuelled by the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway, blocks this degradation and allows Myc to accumulate (Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chou et al., 1995 and Swamy et al., 2016.

claim: In activated lymphocytes the sustained expression of Myc is dependent on the rate of protein synthesis and availability of amino acids.
source: In activated lymphocytes the sustained expression of Myc is also dependent on the rate of protein synthesis and availability of amino acids (Loftus et al., 2018; Sinclair et al., 2013; Swamy et al., 2016; Verbist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The expression of Myc is essential for T cell immune responses.
source: The expression of Myc is essential for T cell immune responses and mature T cells with Myc alleles deleted cannot respond to antigen receptor engagement to proliferate and differentiate (Preston et al., 2015; Trumpp et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mature T cells with Myc alleles deleted cannot respond to antigen receptor engagement to proliferate and differentiate.
source: The expression of Myc is essential for T cell immune responses and mature T cells with Myc alleles deleted cannot respond to antigen receptor engagement to proliferate and differentiate (Preston et al., 2015; Trumpp et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Myc-deficient T cells have defects in glucose and glutamine metabolism.
source: Myc-deficient T cells have defects in glucose and glutamine metabolism (Wang et al., 2011); however, the full molecular details of how Myc regulates T cell metabolic pathways and other aspects of T cell function is not fully understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: There are different models of how Myc works and divergent opinions as to whether or not Myc acts a general amplifier of active gene transcription or has more selective actions.
source: In this context there are different models of how Myc works and divergent opinions as to whether or not Myc acts a general amplifier of active gene transcription (Lewis et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012) or has more selective actions (Sabò et al., 2014; Tesi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies representing different viewpoints.

claim: There is evidence Myc can act post transcriptionally, controlling mRNA cap methylation and broadly enhancing mRNA translation.
source: There is also evidence Myc can act post transcriptionally, controlling mRNA cap methylation and broadly enhancing mRNA translation (Cowling and Cole, 2007; Ruggero, 2009; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There appear to be no universal models of Myc action that can be applied to all cell lineages.
source: The salient point is that there appear to be no universal models of Myc action that can be applied to all cell lineages.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the literature review in the introduction.

claim: Oncogenic Myc mutants control amino acid transporter expression in tumour cells.
source: As an example, it is reported that oncogenic Myc mutants control amino acid transporter expression in tumour cells (Yue et al., 2017) whereas analysis of endogenous Myc function in immune activated primary B cells found no such role (Tesi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2017.

claim: Analysis of endogenous Myc function in immune activated primary B cells found no role in controlling amino acid transporter expression.
source: As an example, it is reported that oncogenic Myc mutants control amino acid transporter expression in tumour cells (Yue et al., 2017) whereas analysis of endogenous Myc function in immune activated primary B cells found no such role (Tesi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tesi et al., 2019.

claim: T cell immune activation is associated with increases in mRNA translation, amino acid transport and protein synthesis all of which shape the execution of the T cell transcriptional program and completely reshape the T cell proteome.
source: T cell immune activation is associated with increases in mRNA translation, amino acid transport and protein synthesis all of which shape the execution of the T cell transcriptional program and completely reshape the T cell proteome (Araki et al., 2017; Geiger et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019; Ricciardi et al., 2018; Sinclair et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Myc-deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells do not substantially increase cell size or proliferate in response to immune activation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 agonist antibodies.
source: As shown previously (Wang et al., 2011), Myc-deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells do not substantially increase cell size or proliferate in response to immune activation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 agonist antibodies (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011 and by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 24 hours post-activation there is minimal impact of autocrine secreted cytokine IL-2 on Myc expression.
source: Moreover, at this time point there is minimal impact of autocrine secreted cytokine IL-2 on Myc expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In contrast to MycWT T cells, CD3/CD28 activated MyccKO T cells fail to increase protein content above the level of naive ex vivo isolated MycWT T cells.
source: The data in Figure 1B show that in contrast to Myc T cells, CD3/CD28 activated MyccKO T cells fail to increase protein content above the level of naive ex vivo isolated MycWT T cells.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The increase in cell biomass that accompanies T cell activation is dependent on Myc.
source: Hence, the increase in cell biomass that accompanies T cell activation is dependent on Myc.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteomics data showing MyccKO cells fail to increase protein content.

claim: The protein content of immune activated MycWT CD4+ T cells was lower than activated CD8+ T cells.
source: Notably, the protein content of immune activated MycWT CD4+ T cells was lower than activated CD8+ T cells and this correlates with higher levels of Myc in immune activated CD8+ versus CD4+ MycWT T cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Higher protein content in activated CD8+ T cells correlates with higher levels of Myc in immune activated CD8+ versus CD4+ MycWT T cells.
source: Notably, the protein content of immune activated MycWT CD4+ T cells was lower than activated CD8+ T cells and this correlates with higher levels of Myc in immune activated CD8+ versus CD4+ MycWT T cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This correlation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: 75% of the protein mass of immune activated MycWT CD4+ and CD8+ T cells comprises 344 and 391 proteins respectively.
source: In this respect a few hundred very abundant proteins are known to account for most cellular mass (Howden et al., 2019; Hukelmann et al., 2016; Ly et al., 2014), with 75% of the protein mass of immune activated MycWT CD4+ and CD8+ T cells comprising 344 and 391 proteins respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by citations and the study's own data.

claim: Myc-deficiency reduced the expression of most, but not all of the abundant proteins that comprise 75% of cellular mass.
source: Myc-deficiency reduced the expression of most, but not all of these abundant proteins (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The impact of Myc loss is striking but clearly selective and not a simple scaled decrease in expression of all proteins.
source: The impact of Myc loss is striking but clearly selective and not a simple scaled decrease in expression of all proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the proteomics analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There are a number of proteins expressed at high levels in naïve cells and downregulated by immune activation in both MycWT and MyccKO T cells, including Kruppel family transcription factors and the IL7 receptor.
source: There are a number of proteins expressed at high levels in naïve cells and downregulated by immune activation in both MycWT and MyccKO T cells (Figure 1G), including Kruppel family transcription factors which maintain pluripotency and cell quiescence (eg Klf2) and growth factors receptors such as the IL7 receptor (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G, H, and I.

claim: There is a subset of ~300–450 proteins that are strongly induced by immune activation irrespective of Myc expression.
source: There is also a subset of ~300–450 proteins that are strongly induced by immune activation irrespective of Myc expression (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: CD69, CD44 and transcription factors cRel and JunB are strongly induced by immune activation irrespective of Myc expression.
source: These include CD69, CD44 and transcription factors cRel and JunB (Figure 1J–M).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1J-M.

claim: The critical transcription factors T-bet and Irf4 were upregulated in immune MyccKO T cells, albeit at reduced levels compared with MycWT T cells.
source: The critical transcription factors T-bet and Irf4 were also upregulated in immune MyccKO T cells, albeit at reduced levels compared with MycWT T cells (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1N-O.

claim: The selective effects of Myc-deficiency on protein expression in activated CD8+ and CD4+ T cells appeared qualitatively similar.
source: The selective effects of Myc-deficiency on protein expression in activated CD8+ and CD4+ T cells appeared qualitatively similar (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: Some proteins were more highly expressed in activated MycWT CD8+ T cells than in MycWT CD4+ T cells, however, Myc-deficiency reduced protein expression down to a similar level in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, therefore giving a larger effect size in CD8+ T cells.
source: These differences reflect that some proteins were more highly expressed in activated MycWT CD8+ T cells than in MycWT CD4+ T cells, however, Myc-deficiency reduced protein expression down to a similar level in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, therefore giving a larger effect size in CD8+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dose-dependent Myc-driven amplification of protein expression is suggested by the observation that CD8+ T cells expressed a higher level of Myc, associated with increased cell biomass.
source: When taken in conjunction with the observation that CD8+ T cells expressed a higher level of Myc (Figure 1C–D), associated with increased cell biomass (Figure 1A–B), this suggests a dose-dependent Myc-driven amplification of protein expression.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the correlation between Myc levels and cell biomass.

claim: Immune activated T cell proteome remodelling comprises both Myc dependent and independent processes.
source: Collectively, these data show that immune activated T cell proteome remodelling comprises both Myc dependent and independent processes and that Myc has a qualitatively similar, but dose-dependent effect on CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proteomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proteomics data presented.

claim: Myc has a qualitatively similar, but dose-dependent effect on CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proteomes.
source: Collectively, these data show that immune activated T cell proteome remodelling comprises both Myc dependent and independent processes and that Myc has a qualitatively similar, but dose-dependent effect on CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proteomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proteomics data presented.

claim: MyccKO T cells increased expression of the glucose transporters Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 (Glut1 and Glut3 respectively) equal to, or exceeding the level seen in MycWT T cells in response to T cell activation.
source: When examining the selective effects of Myc-deficiency on T cell immune activation we observed that MyccKO T cells increased expression of the glucose transporters Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 (Glut1 and Glut3 respectively) equal to, or exceeding the level seen in MycWT T cells in response to T cell activation (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The ability of immune activated MyccKO T cells to upregulate expression of Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 glucose transporters was unexpected as it has been reported that Myc-deficient T cells have abnormal glycolytic metabolism and defective induction of glucose transporter mRNA.
source: The ability of immune activated MyccKO T cells to upregulate expression of Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 glucose transporters was unexpected as it has been reported that Myc-deficient T cells have abnormal glycolytic metabolism and defective induction of glucose transporter mRNA (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and references prior work by Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Slc2a1 has been implicated as a direct transcriptional target of Myc.
source: Moreover, Slc2a1 has been implicated as a direct transcriptional target of Myc (Osthus et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Osthus et al., 2000.

claim: CD3/CD28 triggering increases expression of glycolytic enzymes in both MycWT and MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: In this context, CD3/CD28 triggering increases expression of glycolytic enzymes in both MycWT and MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The cumulative levels of glycolytic enzymes in MyccKO are reduced by 58% and 30% in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells respectively compared with MycWT controls.
source: Although the cumulative levels of glycolytic enzymes in MyccKO are reduced by 58% and 30% in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells respectively compared with MycWT controls, they still comprise a large percentage of the proteomes of immune activated MyccKO T cells (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Glycolytic enzymes still comprise a large percentage of the proteomes of immune activated MyccKO T cells.
source: Although the cumulative levels of glycolytic enzymes in MyccKO are reduced by 58% and 30% in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells respectively compared with MycWT controls, they still comprise a large percentage of the proteomes of immune activated MyccKO T cells (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Myc had a large impact on lactate transporter expression, particularly on the numerically dominant lactate transporter Slc16a1.
source: It was however striking that Myc had a large impact on lactate transporter expression, particularly on the numerically dominant lactate transporter Slc16a1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Lactate transporters control a critical rate limiting step for glycolytic flux.
source: Lactate transporters control a critical rate limiting step for glycolytic flux (Tanner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tanner et al., 2018.

claim: The absence of lactate transporters would prevent lactate export and feedback to suppress glycolytic flux.
source: Their absence would prevent lactate export and feedback to suppress glycolytic flux (Doherty et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doherty et al., 2014.

claim: Slc16a1 expression increases from <10,000 copies per naïve T cell to ~140,000 and~80,000 copies per immune activated CD8+ and CD4+ MycWT T cell respectively.
source: Slc16a1 expression increases from <10,000 copies per naïve T cell to ~140,000 and~80,000 copies per immune activated CD8+ and CD4+ MycWT T cell respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by proteomics data.

claim: Slc16a1 expression in immune activated MyccKO T cells remains equivalent to naive levels.
source: In contrast, Slc16a1 expression in immune activated MyccKO T cells remains equivalent to naive levels (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Control of lactate export is a mechanism whereby Myc controls glycolytic flux in T cells.
source: These data display the selectivity of Myc importance for expression of key components of the glycolysis machinery and point to control of lactate export as a mechanism whereby Myc controls glycolytic flux in T cells.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the data showing Myc control of lactate transporter expression.

claim: Myc controls expression of glutaminase (Gls), Cad and Ppat, the enzymes that control the first steps in glutaminolysis, and pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis respectively.
source: The present data reveal the selectivity of the Myc requirement for expression of important enzymes for glutamine metabolism. Myc controls expression of glutaminase (Gls), Cad and Ppat, the enzymes that control the first steps in glutaminolysis, and pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by proteomics data.

claim: Expression of Gfpt1, the first and rate limiting step in the hexosamine pathway and Glud1, the enzyme that converts glutamate to a-ketoglutarate are still expressed in MyccKO T cells.
source: However, expression of Gfpt1, the first and rate limiting step in the hexosamine pathway and Glud1, the enzyme that converts glutamate to a-ketoglutarate are still expressed in MyccKO T cells (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Myc loss does not prevent loss of the translational repressor Pdcd4 in activated T cells.
source: The data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C shows that Myc loss does not prevent loss of the translational repressor Pdcd4 in activated T cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Myc-deficiency suppressed CD3/CD28 mediated increases in expression of ribosomes, eukaryotic initiation factor 4 (eIF4F) complexes that translate methyl capped mRNAs and EIF2 complexes which controls tRNA transfer to ribosomes.
source: Myc-deficiency did however suppress CD3/CD28 mediated increases in expression of ribosomes, eukaryotic initiation factor 4 (eIF4F) complexes that translate methyl capped mRNAs and EIF2 complexes which controls tRNA transfer to ribosomes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by proteomics data.

claim: An absolutely fundamental requirement for a substantial increase in cell mass is availability of amino acids.
source: Although increasing expression of translational machinery is important, an absolutely fundamental requirement for a substantial increase in cell mass is availability of amino acids (Hosios et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hosios et al., 2016.

claim: The loss of Myc prevents the upregulation of expression of multiple amino acid transporters in activated T cells.
source: Therefore, it is striking that the loss of Myc prevents the upregulation of expression of multiple amino acid transporters in activated T cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The most abundant amino acid transporters expressed on CD3/CD28 activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are Slc7a5, Slc1a5, Slc38a1, Slc38a2 and Slc7a1.
source: The most abundant amino acid transporters expressed on CD3/CD28 activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are Slc7a5 (leucine, methionine, tryptophan), Slc1a5 (glutamine, serine, threonine, alanine), Slc38a1 and Slc38a2 (glutamine, methionine) and Slc7a1(arginine, lysine) (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Naïve T cells have very low levels of amino acid transporters, expressing ~500–2500 copies per cell.
source: Naïve T cells have very low levels of all of these transporters, expressing ~500–2500 copies per cell (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Upon activation, amino acid transporters are some of the most highly induced proteins in MycWT T cells, exhibiting up to 100-fold increases relative to naïve cells.
source: Upon activation, amino acid transporters are some of the most highly induced proteins in MycWT T cells, exhibiting up to 100-fold increases relative to naïve cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Immune activated MyccKO T cells only express amino acid transporters at near naïve levels.
source: In contrast, immune activated MyccKO T cells only express amino acid transporters at near naïve levels (Figure 3A–B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Within 4 hr of T cell activation there is increased system L transport activity in MycWT T cells and this increase is substantially lower in MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Within 4 hr of T cell activation there is already increased system L transport activity in MycWT T cells and this increase is substantially lower in MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the levels of Myc protein expressed by activated T cells and system L amino acid transport capacity.
source: There was also a strong correlation between the levels of Myc protein expressed by activated T cells and system L amino acid transport capacity (Figure 3F) and while system L transport increased substantially over the first 24 hr of T cell activation in MycWT T cells this did not occur in MyccKO T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: System L transport increased substantially over the first 24 hr of T cell activation in MycWT T cells but this did not occur in MyccKO T cells.
source: There was also a strong correlation between the levels of Myc protein expressed by activated T cells and system L amino acid transport capacity (Figure 3F) and while system L transport increased substantially over the first 24 hr of T cell activation in MycWT T cells this did not occur in MyccKO T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myc-deficient T cells fail to increase expression of several key enzymes in metabolic pathways that utilise branch-chain amino acid pathways and methionine.
source: Downstream of Slc7a5 amino acid uptake, Myc-deficient T cells also fail to increase expression of several key enzymes in metabolic pathways that utilise branch-chain amino acid (Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine) pathways and methionine (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Myc plays a critical role in regulating system L amino acid transport and amino acid metabolism in immune activated T cells.
source: Collectively, these data show that Myc plays a critical role in regulating system L amino acid transport and amino acid metabolism in immune activated T cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: The dramatic increase in cell mass associated with normal T cell activation does not occur in immune activated Slc7a5cKO CD4+ T cells.
source: Figure 3G–H shows that the dramatic increase in cell mass associated with normal T cell activation does not occur in immune activated Slc7a5cKO (Cd4Cre+ Slc7a5fl/fl) CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Slc7a5 deficiency has a profound effect on protein expression in immune activated CD4+ T cells.
source: These data show Slc7a5 deficiency, similar to Myc deficiency, has a profound effect on protein expression in immune activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3I.

claim: Slc7a5cKO T cells still respond to antigen receptor activation to downregulate a subset of naïve T cell proteins and can still upregulate expression of a small subset of proteins.
source: Slc7a5cKO T cells still respond to antigen receptor activation to downregulate a subset of naïve T cell proteins and can still upregulate expression of a small subset of proteins (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3I.

claim: There is a striking overlap in proteins that were both Myc and Slc7a5 regulated.
source: The data show a striking overlap in proteins that were both Myc and Slc7a5 regulated (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3J.

claim: Most of the overlap between Myc and Slc7a5 regulated proteins was in proteins that were reduced in response to Myc or Slc7a5 deficiency.
source: Most of this overlap was in proteins that were reduced in response to Myc or Slc7a5 deficiency (Figure 3K), including translational machinery such as ribosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Slc7a5-deficiency does not completely phenocopy the effects of Myc-deficiency.
source: Although there is a large degree of overlap in the proteomics data, Slc7a5-deficiency does not completely phenocopy the effects of Myc-deficiency.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by the proteomics comparison.

claim: Induction of proteins such as the glucose transporter Slc2a3 and effector molecules like Granzyme B and IFNγ exhibit a more severe defect in Slc7a5cKO T cells compared to MyccKO T cells.
source: Induction of proteins such as the glucose transporter Slc2a3 (Figure 2B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C) and effector molecules like Granzyme B and IFNγ (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D–E) exhibit a more severe defect in Slc7a5cKO T cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: The more severe defect in Slc7a5cKO T cells is likely due to the lack of basal-level amino acid transport in naïve Slc7a5cKO T cells which is not deficient in naïve MyccKO T cells.
source: This is likely due to the lack of basal-level amino acid transport in naïve Slc7a5cKO T cells which is not deficient in naïve MyccKO T cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the data in Figure 3C.

claim: Deficiency in a single Myc controlled amino acid transporter, Slc7a5, largely mimics the phenotype of MyccKO T cells, preventing T cell growth and selectively controlling proteome remodelling.
source: Overall, deficiency in a single Myc controlled amino acid transporter, Slc7a5, largely does mimic the phenotype of MyccKO T cells, preventing T cell growth and selectively controlling proteome remodelling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative proteomics data.

claim: Single cell RNAseq analysis of antigen activated OT1 CD8+ T cells shows a strong correlation at the single cell level of Myc mRNA expression and expression of mRNA for Slc7a5, Slc7a1 and Slc1a5.
source: Single cell RNAseq analysis of antigen activated OT1 CD8+ T cells (Richard et al., 2018) shows a strong correlation at the single cell level of Myc mRNA expression and expression of mRNA for Slc7a5, Slc7a1 and Slc1a5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A and citation to Richard et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of Myc mRNA clearly precedes increased expression of mRNA for Slc7a5 and Slc1a5.
source: Expression of Myc mRNA clearly precedes increased expression of mRNA for Slc7a5 and Slc1a5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: In a proteomics time course of OT1 CD8+ T cell activation, expression of Myc protein precedes antigen induced increases in expression of most amino acid transporters.
source: More importantly, in a proteomics time course of OT1 CD8+ T cell activation, expression of Myc protein precedes antigen induced increases in expression of most amino acid transporters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of amino acid transporters increases gradually over time during T cell activation.
source: Proteomics data shows that expression of amino acid transporters increases gradually over time (Figure 4B), and Kyn uptake experiments confirm that this increase in transporter number corresponds with higher system L uptake (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD3/CD28 activation of MycWT CD4+ and CD8+ T cells drives increases in Slc7a5, Slc1a5 and Slc7a1 mRNA.
source: CD3/CD28 activation of MycWT CD4+ and CD8+ T cells drives increases in Slc7a5, Slc1a5 and Slc7a1 mRNA, whereas activated MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells do not increase expression of Slc7a5 or Slc1a5 mRNA and show reduced expression of Slc7a1 mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Activated MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells do not increase expression of Slc7a5 or Slc1a5 mRNA and show reduced expression of Slc7a1 mRNA.
source: CD3/CD28 activation of MycWT CD4+ and CD8+ T cells drives increases in Slc7a5, Slc1a5 and Slc7a1 mRNA, whereas activated MyccKO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells do not increase expression of Slc7a5 or Slc1a5 mRNA and show reduced expression of Slc7a1 mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Previous studies have shown that Slc7a5 is required for expression of Myc protein (but not mRNA) in activated CD8+ T cells.
source: However one possible inconsistency is that previous studies have shown that Slc7a5 is required for expression of Myc protein (but not mRNA) in activated CD8+ T cells (Sinclair et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sinclair et al., 2013.

claim: Slc7a5 is not required for the immediate and rapid upregulation of Myc expression that accompanies T cell activation but is required for activated T cells to sustain Myc protein.
source: These data (Figure 4D) show that Slc7a5 is not required for the immediate and rapid upregulation of Myc expression that accompanies T cell activation but is required for activated T cells to sustain Myc protein.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Rapamycin treatment had very little impact on expression of Myc protein after 4 hr of T cell activation but did reduce Myc expression after 24 hr.
source: The data show that rapamycin treatment had very little impact on expression of Myc protein after 4 hr of T cell activation but did reduce Myc expression after 24 hr (Figure 4E), consistent with the results seen in Slc7a5cKO T cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4E and Figure 4D.

claim: The presence of external amino acids is necessary for expression of Myc protein, with T cells activated in amino acid-free media being unable to express Myc protein despite increasing the activation marker CD69.
source: Although Slc7a5 deficiency or mTORC1 inhibition alone was insufficient to prevent Myc induction, the presence of external amino acids is necessary for expression of Myc protein, with T cells activated in amino acid-free media being unable to express Myc protein despite increasing the activation marker CD69 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Deficiency of a single amino acid from the media, such as glutamine, methionine or leucine leads to a reduction in Myc levels but does not prevent its expression.
source: Deficiency of a single amino acid from the media, such as glutamine, methionine or leucine leads to a reduction in Myc levels but does not prevent its expression (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Myc driven increase in amino acid transport triggers a positive feedforward loop supporting its own continued expression which in turn drives and sustains further increases in amino acid transport.
source: Myc driven increase in amino acid transport thus triggers a positive feedforward loop supporting its own continued expression which in turn drives and sustains further increases in amino acid transport.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data showing the relationship between Myc and amino acid transport.

claim: Myc was required for the increase in expression of important metabolic pathway proteins such as glutamine transporters and glutaminase, and lactate transporters.
source: Myc was required for the increase in expression of important metabolic pathway proteins; for example, glutamine transporters and glutaminase, key proteins controlling the first steps of glutaminolysis (Newsholme et al., 1985); and lactate transporters, a major rate determining step for glycolytic flux (Tanner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the proteomics data and citations.

claim: Expression of many key metabolic enzymes for both glutaminolysis and glycolysis can still occur in immune activated Myc null T cells.
source: However, the current data also show that expression of many key metabolic enzymes for both glutaminolysis and glycolysis can still occur in immune activated Myc null T cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the proteomics data.

claim: Myc was not required for protein expression of the glucose transporters Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 in activated T cells.
source: In particular, in the context of glucose metabolism an unexpected observation was that Myc was not required for protein expression of the glucose transporters Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 in activated T cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the proteomics data.

claim: The observation that Myc was not required for glucose transporter protein expression was surprising, given previous observations that Myc deletion reduced Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 mRNA.
source: This was surprising, given previous observations that Myc deletion reduced Slc2a1 and Slc2a3 mRNA (Wang et al., 2011) and highlights the value of a proteomics approach to quantify the expression patterns of proteins where there may be a disconnect between mRNA and protein expression due to translational regulation (Ricciardi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The differential control of glucose and lactate transporters by Myc reveals that upregulation of metabolic pathways during T cell activation is more complex than a simple activation switch or amplifier mediated by a single transcription factor.
source: The expression of both glucose and lactate transporters are key for glycolytic flux (Tanner et al., 2018) and the fact that these are differentially controlled by Myc reveals that upregulation of metabolic pathways during T cell activation is more complex than a simple activation switch or amplifier mediated by a single transcription factor (Nie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement in the discussion based on the data and citations.

claim: T cell metabolic reprogramming requires the coordination of Myc expression with other signalling pathways.
source: The data gives molecular insight into why Myc is so important for T cell glutamine metabolism and glycolysis but they also reveal that T cell metabolic reprogramming requires the coordination of Myc expression with other signalling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the data.

claim: Activation of mTORc1 is not required for Myc expression in activated T cell but does have a substantive effect on the expression of glucose transporter protein.
source: In this respect we have shown recently that activation of mTORc1 is not required for Myc expression in activated T cell but does have a substantive effect on the expression of glucose transporter protein (Howden et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Howden et al., 2019.

claim: A primary function of Myc is to control expression of the amino acid transporters, inducing a positive feedforward loop to sustain Myc levels in activated T cells.
source: One key conclusion from the present data is that a primary function of Myc is to control expression of the amino acid transporters, inducing a positive feedforward loop to sustain Myc levels in activated T cells.
evidence: This is a key conclusion stated in the discussion based on the data.

claim: Myc was only necessary for immune activation associated increases in amino acid transporter expression.
source: A salient point is that Myc was only necessary for immune activation associated increases in amino acid transporter expression.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data.

claim: The absence of Myc did not impinge on the low basal levels of amino acid transport through the system L transporter seen in naïve T cells.
source: The absence of Myc did not impinge on the low basal levels of amino acid transport through the system L transporter seen in naïve T cells and it was clear from the proteomic data that Myc null T cells still had some capacity to increase expression of key proteins.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data.

claim: The inability of Myc null T cells to increase amino acid transport aligns with previous metabolomic data that Myc null cells have decreased levels of intracellular amino acids.
source: The inability of Myc null T cells to increase amino acid transport aligns with previous metabolomic data that Myc null cells have decreased levels of intracellular amino acids (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The loss of amino acid transporter induction in Myc null T cells would prevent the increases in expression of the protein biosynthetic machinery as well as preventing uptake of the raw material required to synthesise protein.
source: The loss of amino acid transporter induction in Myc null T cells would also prevent the increases in expression of the protein biosynthetic machinery as well as preventing uptake of the raw material required to synthesise protein.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement in the discussion based on the data.

claim: The importance of Myc induction of amino acid transporters for T cell activation is particularly highlighted by the large effect of deleting just one of the Myc controlled amino acid transporters, Slc7a5, on the T cell proteome.
source: The importance of Myc induction of amino acid transporters for T cell activation is particularly highlighted by the large effect of deleting just one of the Myc controlled amino acid transporters, Slc7a5, on the T cell proteome, which almost phenocopies the effects of Myc deletion itself.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the comparative proteomics data.

claim: Slc7a5 transports multiple large neutral amino acids including Leucine, Phenylalanine and Tryptophan.
source: The impact of the loss of a single Myc controlled amino acid transporter was remarkable and reflects that Slc7a5 transports multiple large neutral amino acids including Leucine, Phenylalanine and Tryptophan.
evidence: This is a statement of known transporter function in the discussion.

claim: Slc7a5 is the major T cell transporter for Methionine, the predominant 'start' amino acid used to initiate polypeptide synthesis during mRNA translation.
source: Myc control of Slc7a5 expression would be particularly important for protein synthesis as Slc7a5 is also the major T cell transporter for Methionine, the predominant 'start' amino acid used to initiate polypeptide synthesis during mRNA translation (Sinclair et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Myc control of Slc7a5 would have indirect consequences for the expression of thousands of proteins in immune activated T cells and could underpin the ability of Myc to regulate multiple biosynthetic, bioenergetic and epigenetic processes in T cells.
source: These data highlight how Myc control of even one amino acid transporter, Slc7a5, would have indirect consequences for the expression of thousands of proteins in immune activated T cells and could underpin the ability of Myc to regulate multiple biosynthetic, bioenergetic and epigenetic processes in T cells.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretive statement in the discussion based on the data.
